title: Development legitimacy depends increasingly on how change is negotiated, especially by groups that bear its losses
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11234, Process Legitimacy and Development: Analytical Framings, Implications, and Applications
geography: Development-policy and institutional-reform contexts across societal, local, national and international levels

observations.period: October 2025 working paper; legitimacy of social change

fairness.value: the legitimacy of social change depends partly on whether the way change is pursued is perceived as legitimate by those most affected, especially those who lose

drivers.value: the paper identifies constituent drivers and mechanisms through which process legitimacy is established, consolidated, challenged and altered

risk.value: development interventions face legitimacy risks when they fail to navigate contested processes and affected-group perceptions

observations.method: World Bank policy research working paper developing an analytical framework from prior process-legitimacy concepts and applications in development practice.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a conceptual and applied framework, not a representative perception survey, causal evaluation or universal legitimacy index.
observations.subgroup: People affected by development change, including groups that bear losses; societal groups, local communities, authorities, elites, national actors and international institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Procedural fairness can improve acceptance without making an unequal outcome substantively fair; participation can also be captured by powerful actors.

observations.period: October 2025 working paper; four levels of legitimacy contestation

denominator.unit: levels of legitimacy contest identified by the paper

contests.value: legitimacy contests occur between societal groups, elite factions, national and local authorities, and national and global actors

verticality.value: legitimacy is not only a citizen-state question; it also moves across horizontal group relations and multiple levels of authority

implication.value: the typology helps identify risks when interventions overlook who has authority, voice, losses or competing goals

observations.method: Actor-based analytical model of legitimacy contests in development and institutional change.
observations.uncertainty: The four-level typology organizes possible disputes but does not measure the frequency, intensity or outcome of contests across countries.
observations.subgroup: Communities, identity groups, elites, local governments, national governments, donors, international organizations, firms and affected publics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Multi-level analysis can reveal conflict pathways while making responsibility diffuse and negotiation slow, especially when urgent action is required.

observations.period: October 2025 working paper; negotiation and shared understanding

negotiation.value: development interventions can help navigate legitimacy contests by creating constructive spaces for negotiation

shared_goals.value: processes can support the gradual emergence of shared understanding around legitimate goals and procedures

institutional_route.value: legitimacy is treated as something that can be consolidated or challenged through ongoing interaction rather than granted once at project approval

observations.method: Analytical synthesis connecting legitimacy drivers, contestation and development-intervention design.
observations.uncertainty: The proposed negotiation route is not an intervention effect estimate and does not specify a universal forum, timeline or representation rule.
observations.subgroup: Affected residents, project beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries, implementing agencies, local authorities, donors, firms and civil-society organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Negotiation spaces can legitimize delay, reproduce power asymmetries or shift responsibility for politically difficult trade-offs onto participants.

observations.period: October 2025 working paper; process legitimacy and implementation risk

policy_effectiveness.value: perceived procedural legitimacy is presented as relevant to whether development change can proceed and retain cooperation

affected_losses.value: groups that lose from social change are treated as central to legitimacy analysis rather than as residual opposition

accountability.value: the framework directs attention to representation, negotiation, authority and contestation alongside material project outputs

observations.method: Policy-oriented analytical paper with applications to development practice and institutional reform.
observations.uncertainty: The paper does not show that procedural legitimacy guarantees compliance, project delivery, trust or equitable outcomes, and it does not replace outcome or distributional evaluation.
observations.subgroup: Affected groups, implementing institutions, local and national authorities, donors, international actors, firms and communities with unequal bargaining power.
observations.counterinterpretation: A project can be procedurally legitimate to some actors and illegitimate to others; legitimacy claims must remain open to contestation and material accountability.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank publication record for Policy Research Working Paper 11234.
World Bank program context linking process legitimacy to participatory, people-centred work in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

boundary: This record adds a process-legitimacy route linking how development change is pursued to perceived fairness, representation, contestation, negotiation, cooperation, institutional trust and implementation risk. It is a 2025 conceptual and applied World Bank working paper, not a respondent-level legitimacy dataset, causal project evaluation, current public-opinion estimate or proof that participatory processes produce equitable outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank PDF and publication record were reviewed for the process-legitimacy framework, affected-group lens, four-level contest typology, negotiation pathway and implementation boundaries.
